India brought a complaint to the young United Nations in 1946: the treatment of people of Indian origin in the Union of South Africa. The General Assembly took up the charge in Resolution 44, adopted on 8 December 1946. It was one of the first times the Assembly judged how a member state treated people inside its own borders.

The Assembly states that the treatment has harmed friendly ties between India and South Africa, and that ties will worsen without a fair settlement. It holds that the treatment must match the deals struck between the two states and the pledges of the UN Charter. Both states must report back at the next session.
un-ga-res-a-69-44:
Missiles that can carry mass-kill warheads are the target of Resolution A/69/44, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. The spread of such ballistic missiles, it says, feeds growing strains on safety at home and abroad. The text recalls Assembly votes on the point since 2004 and the UN's duty, under the Charter, to guard peace.

Praise goes to the Hague Code of Conduct against Ballistic Missile Proliferation, adopted at The Hague on 25 November 2002. The code asks states to show restraint and to share word of their missile plans in advance. Such open steps, the Assembly holds, build trust and help curb the spread of the missiles themselves.

The Council now asks the Secretary-General to call a special session of the Assembly, under Article 20 of the Charter, to weigh the future rule of Palestine anew.

The text sets the mission's tasks: guard government sites and airports, protect aid convoys, and help train Somali security forces. It also calls on other states to fund and supply the effort. Readers get the founding terms of AMISOM, the African-led mission that became a central actor in Somalia's long war.

Barbara Davids, David Reiner, Shanda Birkeland, and co-authors catalogued a fresh family of genes in a gut parasite in 2006. Giardia makes people sick with diarrhea worldwide, and it survives outside the body as a hard cyst. Its surface proteins, the VSPs, were well studied; this team looked beyond them.

They found a new family of giardial genes coding for cysteine-rich proteins that are not VSPs, plus a novel cyst protein involved in the parasite's survival shell. New surface and cyst parts are candidate targets for drugs and diagnostics, since they sit where the parasite meets its host. The paper extends the known toolkit of one of humanity's most common parasites.
gregory-great-morals-on-job-vol-1-1844:
Pope Gregory the Great wrote his Morals on the Book of Job, the Moralia in Job, in the late 500s, near the start of his time as pope. Volume one of the Rev. James Bliss English translation came out in 1844 in the Library of the Fathers series. It holds Parts One and Two of Gregory's huge work.

Gregory reads Job line by line and draws three layers from the text: the plain story, a picture of Christ and the church, and a lesson for the reader's own conduct. Job's patience under loss becomes a guide for prayer, humility, and trust. Medieval readers treated the Moralia as a handbook of the inner life.

Security Council Resolution 744, adopted on February 25, 1992, recommended San Marino for membership in the United Nations. The tiny republic, ringed by Italy, counts itself the oldest surviving republic in the world, with roots in the year 301. Size had long kept it outside the world body, but the end of the Cold War opened the door to Europe's small states.

The Assembly admitted San Marino on March 2, 1992. The council's text is brief and formal, like all admission votes of that season. For San Marino, the seat carried a point of pride: a state older than most kingdoms at last took the same formal place as the largest powers in the General Assembly hall.

The booklet runs to sixty-six numbered pages, with front and back matter and some fifty pages of pictures and appendices. Lieutenant William Rigdon prepared it, and Rear Admiral Wilson Brown approved it. Inside are the President's party list, an itinerary, sea and air travel charts, a foreword, and the log itself. Eleven appendices follow, from a citation for General Eisenhower to the Cairo and Tehran communiqués.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d344:
Alexander Kirk, the American minister in Egypt, wrote a short secret memorandum at Cairo on 26 November 1943 about his custody of the Cairo communiqué. It records a small errand at the center of the conference's secrecy.

That afternoon Harry Hopkins handed Kirk a copy of the communiqué on the Anglo-American-Chinese talks and asked him to hold it until instructions came from Tehran about its release. The timing was undecided, but Kirk would get twenty-four hours' notice so the three countries could publish at the same moment. Kirk was also to notify the Chinese legation when the word came. His own task, as he summed it up, was simply to see that American correspondents in Cairo received the text through the Office of War Information.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d444:
Marked with a footnote in the printed volume, this second set of Combined Chiefs of Staff minutes from December 5, 1943 covers another session of the joint American-British command at Cairo. The Second Cairo Conference was then deciding the next phase of the war against Germany and Japan. The State Department later published the record in its Cairo-Tehran volume.

Session minutes preserve the order of business, the officers' exchanges, and the conclusions reached before the chiefs reported upward to Roosevelt and Churchill. Having two records from one day shows how much was pressed into these meetings. For a reader tracing how Allied plans took final shape, that density is the point.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d544:
Secretary of State Cordell Hull wrote to President Roosevelt on January 11, 1944, keeping up the steady channel between the department and the White House. The message appears in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran conference volume, among the follow-up papers of the new year.

Hull's January traffic with Roosevelt mixed the conferences' unfinished business with the planning of the postwar order, a subject Hull cared about deeply. The Secretary had built his reputation on patient, formal diplomacy, the opposite of summit improvisation. For readers, the message shows the permanent government digesting the leaders' December decisions and fitting them into policy that could last.
frus-1944-quebec-d44:

They stated what Britain needed from the conference. For readers, the message marks a final approach. The Prime Minister was at sea or about to sail. The agenda for the meeting was effectively set. Only the arguments in person remained.
frus-1944-quebec-d144:

His own chiefs believed a vigorous attack, pressed with everything available, should force the enemy into the Po Valley.

The president stressed destroying German forces while they were within grasp, lest divisions escape to other fronts. He was confident Eisenhower would be satisfied that the Mediterranean effort was mauling troops that might otherwise face him. On the future use of Wilson's armies, Roosevelt suspended decision until the campaign's results were known. Trieste and Istria, he said, they would renew at Octagon, the Quebec meeting.
frus-1944-quebec-d244:
Hull asked Roosevelt for instructions on the French lend-lease agreement on September 11, 1944. The sticking point was Jean Monnet's request for industrial items to restart French production for the civil population. Under the July 15 memorandum Roosevelt had approved, such long-life industrial goods could go on credit only if necessary to the war in Europe or to forces just after an armistice.

Applied now, Hull wrote, that rule flatly rejected Monnet's program of over a billion dollars in industrial items. He recommended neither rejection nor approval. Instead, a list mechanism would leave the president complete discretion, item by item, as French behavior warranted. The Foreign Economic Administration would submit proposed French programs to Roosevelt before they joined the list.

frus-1945-malta-yalta-d144:

Mikolajczyk protests the pressure on his government to accept the Curzon Line at once, without any reservations. All his work, he writes, has aimed at Polish-Soviet understanding, for Poland's sake and for the common cause. Yet his nation would feel terribly deceived, he warns, if this were the answer to its sacrifices and its unbroken part in the war. He asks the President for a reply and decisions at the earliest possible moment.

The United States should take the lead in helping China build a strong, stable, and unified government. Such a China could be the chief steadying force in the Far East. frus-1945-malta-yalta-d344:
Bremen and Bremerhaven would stay under full American control, under an agreement the Combined Chiefs of Staff approved at Yalta in February 1945. The enclave, drawn on an attached map, covered the ports and their ground. American military government would run it, including disarmament and the breaking up of German war power there.

At the same time, the American commander was to follow the broad policies used in the British zone around it. He kept the right to depart from them on military grounds when he judged it needful. Transit rights each way — American stores southward, British movement toward Austria — complete the bargain.

A whole frontier might fall to Britain alone, and London disliked the prospect in this statement of February 10, 1945. If British proposals for occupation zones in Austria were approved, the entire Austro-Yugoslav frontier would be a British responsibility. Yugoslavia had not asked to alter the Styrian stretch. But it had advanced claims to Klagenfurt and parts of Carinthia, lost in the plebiscite of 1919.

Action might be needed to resist Yugoslav efforts to press those claims. Yugoslav partisans might also advance into Carinthia during operations and hold ground there. For Britain to stand alone in such a quarrel, the paper argues, would be invidious. The warning proved exact within months.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d44:

It is document 44 in the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference, sent as the Allied leaders arranged their first meeting since Germany's surrender. Churchill's own plans, he says, depend on the date Truman picks.

Churchill also raises a point of pride and fairness. He reports good talks with Truman's envoy Joseph Davies, but warns he will not attend a meeting that simply continues a private conference between Truman and Stalin. The three leaders, he insists, should meet at the same time and on equal terms. He closes by saying he looks forward to meeting Truman in person for the first time.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d144:

Without that change, he warned, every other measure would be a brief patch at best. The aim was a Germany no longer dangerous to its neighbors. tob-4244:

tob-4144:
Griffith's verse Ramayana opens with volume one in 1870, and India's beloved epic found its English singer. Prince Rama, exiled from his father's court through a queen's demand, withdraws to the forest with his wife Sita and brother Lakshmana. There the demon king Ravana steals Sita away to Lanka.

tob-13144:

podcast-dannyjones-SiBFtwbyv44:

podcast-joerogan-_bN4spt3744:

chambers-vestiges-1844:
Vestiges of the Natural History of Creation appeared anonymously in 1844 and became a sensation. Its author, revealed only after his death, was Robert Chambers, an Edinburgh publisher. The book popularized evolution, human evolution included, fifteen years before Darwin's Origin of Species.

Chambers argues that all life, man included, rose by natural law from simple beginnings, as planets form and species unfold. The science is shaky in places, but the sweep carried thousands of readers into deep time. Clergy denounced it; drawing rooms devoured it; Darwin read the storm and took care to build his own case stronger. The book Darwin had to answer still repays reading.
quicherat-proces-jeanne-darc-vol2-1844:
Quicherat's second volume, printed in 1844, carries his Joan of Arc edition from sentence toward review. It completes the papers of the 1431 condemnation trial. It then opens the rehabilitation proceedings of 1455 and 1456, a full generation later.

The shift in the records is stark: the same deeds are read first as crimes, then as grounds for honor. Judges and clerks of the 1450s re-open each charge the first court had pressed. The volume bridges the fire at Rouen and the inquiry that undid its verdict. Readers watch a famous case reverse itself in its own papers.
poe-mesmeric-revelation-1844:
Edgar Allan Poe set Mesmeric Revelation in print in 1844. The form is a death bed talk held by art. A man in a mesmeric trance, close to death, speaks with the scribe. He tells what God, stuff, and the soul are past the veil of flesh.

Stuff is not dead, the voice holds, but one fine spread of force. Each grain of it can think, feel, and at last join the whole. Death is a shift, not an end, in this strange scheme. The tale is the most famed of Poe's works on the mesmeric creed.
dumas-three-musketeers-1844:
Alexandre Dumas published The Three Musketeers in 1844, in serial form in a Paris paper. The swashbuckling tale of d'Artagnan and his three friends became a byword for adventure in France. Its motto, all for one and one for all, is known far beyond the book.

Young d'Artagnan rides to Paris with a letter, a horse, and dreams of the King's Musketeers. He falls in with Athos, Porthos, and Aramis, and duels become brotherhood in a single day. Queen Anne's diamond studs, Richelieu's plots, and the spy Milady drive the swift intrigue along. The siege of La Rochelle gives the private vendettas a grand public stage of war. Dumas's pace, humor, and swordplay still set the bar for historical adventure tales.
dumas-count-of-monte-cristo-1844:
Alexandre Dumas published The Count of Monte Cristo in 1844, in serial form in Paris. The vast tale of betrayal and revenge became one of the world's most popular novels ever. Dumas drew its germ from a police file tale of a man falsely jailed for years.

Edmond Dantès, a young sailor, is jailed on his wedding day by rivals' false charges. In the Château d'If, Abbé Faria teaches him and tells of a vast treasure on Monte Cristo. Dantès escapes, finds the gold, and returns as the Count to ruin his three betrayers. Each revenge is patient, rich, and exact, yet mercy checks his hand at the brink. The book's grip on readers, from schoolboys to statesmen, has never loosened since 1844.
dumas-corsican-brothers-1844:
Alexandre Dumas published The Corsican Brothers in 1844, here in Henry Frith's English translation. The eerie tale is the definitive literary treatment of the Corsican blood feud in fiction. Dumas had toured Corsica and filled the tale with its wild hills and stern codes.

Twin brothers, joined at birth and split by surgery, still share each other's pains across distance. One lives a Paris dandy, the other a mountain man bound to vendetta and honor in Corsica. A duel over a woman in Paris is felt, wound for wound, by the brother at home. The surviving twin takes up the feud, and the debt of blood is paid in full. Frith's version kept the tale a staple of English Gothic and sensation shelves.
dumas-regents-daughter-1844:
Alexandre Dumas published The Regent's Daughter in 1844, opening his Regency cycle of historical romance. The tale retells the Cellamare conspiracy against the Regent, Philippe d'Orléans, in early 1700s France. It appeared the same year as The Three Musketeers, in Dumas's flood of serial triumphs then.

Gaston de Chanlay, a Breton noble, joins a Spanish-backed plot to kidnap the Regent in Paris. He loves Hélène, a convent girl who proves to be the Regent's own hidden daughter in secret. Duty to the plot and love for Hélène tear the young conspirator in two at Paris. The Regent's mercy and the block await the plotters in a close of mixed grace. Dumas finds pathos in a minor plot that most histories pass in a page.
emerson-essays-second-series-1844:
Ralph Waldo Emerson published Essays: Second Series in 1844, with The Poet and Experience inside. The set is the mature statement of transcendentalist aesthetics in Emerson's evolving and deepening public thought. Grief for his dead son darkens Experience, giving the later essays a chastened, autumnal tone throughout them.

The Poet calls for an American bard who will sing the facts of farms, trades, and rivers. Experience asks what life teaches when sorrow shows how little the soul can truly hold fast. Character, Manners, and Gifts weigh how spirit shows in conduct, breeding, and the things we give. Emerson's sentences here are denser, more oracular, and less sure than in the first bright series. Whitman and later poets took The Poet as a personal commission to write America.
thackeray-barry-lyndon-1844:
William Makepeace Thackeray published Barry Lyndon in 1844, a novel in the form of a rogue's memoir. Redmond Barry is an Irish adventurer who tells his own story with great pride. He serves as a soldier, deserts, and becomes a gambler and cheat across Europe. He marries a rich widow to gain rank and wealth.

Barry boasts even as his schemes ruin others and himself. Thackeray lets the narrator expose his own vanity on every page. The book first appeared as The Luck of Barry Lyndon in a magazine. Its unreliable narrator was ahead of its time. Readers now prize its irony and pace.
snorri-heimskringla-laing-1844:
Samuel Laing published The Heimskringla; Or, Chronicle of the Kings of Norway in 1844, the first English translation of Snorri Sturluson's kings' sagas. Snorri, an Icelandic poet and chieftain, wrote the Heimskringla in the 1200s. It tells the story of Norway's kings from mythic times to his own age.

Sagas of kings such as Olaf Tryggvason, Saint Olaf, and Harald Hardrada fill the chronicle, drawn from poems and oral memory. Battles, voyages, and feuds move at saga pace, terse and vivid. Laing's version founded the study of Norse history in English. Readers who want the Vikings in their own tradition's telling still start with Snorri.
faraday-experimental-researches-vol2-184:
Volume 2 of Faraday's Experimental Researches in Electricity appeared in 1844, holding Series 15 through 19. Michael Faraday's researches had by then moved from the first shock of induction toward the deep laws of electric action in matter. The papers here continue his electrochemical work.

Faraday tested how currents pass through gases and liquids and how electricity relates to chemical change. He also probed the nature of induction through different materials, work that fed his growing picture of lines of force. That picture later became the field concept in the hands of Maxwell. Volume 2 shows the middle stage of the research program that Volume 1 began and Volume 3 completed.
schiller-poems-first-period-1844:
The Poems of Schiller: First Period gathers the young Schiller's lyrics in the Bohn Standard Library translation. The poems date from his stormy first years as a writer, before Weimar classicism calmed his style. Some of them stand inside his early play The Robbers, sung or quoted by its outlaws.

Love, rage at tyrants, and wild joy in nature drive these early pieces. The verse is rough, bold, and full of youthful excess by design. Readers can hear the voice that shocked Germany in 1781 taking shape. The Bohn set sorted Schiller's poems by period so English readers could trace his growth. This first volume gives the raw material of the later master.
schiller-poems-second-period-1844:
Schiller's middle years produced the poems in this second-period volume of the Bohn translation. By then Schiller had settled into study, friendship with Goethe, and steady fame. The Song of the Bell, his most loved long poem, belongs to this era of his work.

In that poem the casting of a church bell frames the whole course of a human life. Birth, love, work, loss, and death pass in its stanzas like scenes at a foundry. Other pieces here treat art, gods, and the dignity of man. The voice is calmer than the young rebel's, but the moral fire remains. Lyric readers rank this period at the height of Schiller's power.
schiller-poems-suppressed-1844:
Schiller chose not to reprint some of his early poems, and the Bohn editors gathered those pieces as the Suppressed Poems. They complete the four-volume English set of his poetry. In them the young writer speaks without the guard he later kept on his work.

The suppressed pieces show sharper satire, bolder feeling, and rougher craft than he later allowed. Some attack named targets of his youth with open scorn. Others try forms and tones he soon outgrew and disowned. Scholars value the set because it shows growth honestly, false starts included. English readers in the Bohn volumes could meet the whole Schiller, not only the polished classic. The volume rewards those who like a poet unbuttoned.
schiller-poems-third-period-1844:
The late poems in this third-period Bohn volume include Schiller's great ballads of his Weimar years. The Diver sends a young page to the sea floor for a king's golden cup, twice. The Glove tests a lady's love with a cruel and famous gesture among wild beasts.

The tales move swiftly, with clear scenes and ringing morals that never preach. Generations of German schoolchildren learned them by heart. berkeley-siris-1744:
Siris, from 1744, is George Berkeley's strangest and most wide-ranging late work. Its full title promises a chain of philosophical reflexions and inquiries. The subject at the chain's foot is tar water, a folk tonic of pine tar stirred in water. Berkeley praised it as a cure for fevers and ills, in verse and prose alike.

All 367 sections are here, and the chain climbs far from the tonic bottle. Berkeley rises through chemistry and the fine fluid called aether to Plato, the Trinity, and God himself. The book joins medicine, physics, and theology in one ascending argument. It is the old immaterialist's last word, and his boldest.
mill-essays-unsettled-questions-1844:
John Stuart Mill wrote his Essays on Some Unsettled Questions of Political Economy in 1829 and 1830. He published them only in 1844, when his name could carry them. The essays ask how the science of economics itself should work. What is its method, and how should its terms be defined?

Mill argues that political economy reasons from known tendencies of human nature. Its laws hold as tendencies, not as clockwork certainties. That careful account of method underlies his later Principles of Political Economy. The Gutenberg text keeps the five essays whole. Readers meet the young Mill thinking about thinking. sandby-mesmerism-opponents-1844:
George Sandby answered mesmerism's first British critics in Mesmerism and Its Opponents, from 1844. Sandby was a clergyman who had watched mesmeric cures at close range. His narrative of cases replies to doctors and editors who scorned the practice. Detailed case histories carry the weight of his argument.

Patients relieved of pain and fits tell their own part in his pages. The book records the first wave of English controversy over mesmerism. Charges of fraud and folly met charges of closed minds. Sandby writes as a witness more than a theorist. His cases fed the movement's early defense. The volume is a primary record of a public fight.
zoist-vol-02-1844:
Volume two of The Zoist covers April 1844 to January 1845. Elliotson's journal presses on with its twin subjects, cerebral physiology and mesmerism. Case reports arrive from doctors across Britain who tried the mesmeric sleep. Operations without pain hold pride of place in the reports.

Somnambulists and their strange sight supply the journal's wonders. Critics in the medical press trade blows with Elliotson's circle in print. The journal binds those fights beside the clinical record. Across thirteen volumes the set forms the English movement's full archive. Volume two shows the fight at full heat. Surgeons, patients, and skeptics all speak here. The record stays primary and direct.
plos-pone-0003444:

plos-pone-0003544:

plos-pone-0003644:

plos-pone-0003744:

plos-pone-0003844:
Lindsey N. Shaw, Catharina Lindholm, Tomasz K. Prajsnar, and colleagues published this bacteria study in PLOS ONE in 2008. plos-pone-0003944:
Satoshi Habuchi, Hidekazu Tsutsui, Anna B. Kochaniak, and co-authors presented a switchable glowing protein in 2008. Glowing proteins that turn on and off with light had lately widened cell imaging. Their PLOS ONE article describes mKikGR, a single-unit version that switches with light. A single-unit tag behaves more like the protein it labels. The new tool aids fine imaging of movement inside living cells. It adds a cleaner option to the molecular biology toolkit.
plos-pone-0004044:
Adrian L. Melott searched fossil records for long cycles in life history in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. The Paleobiology Database holds marine invertebrate fossil counts through time. A real cycle would link Earth's history to life's ups and downs. It was printed in PLOS ONE, where the full text stays free to read.
plos-pone-0004144:
Feng-Ping Lu, Kun-Pei Lin, and Hsu-Ko Kuo published this review in PLOS ONE in 2009. Earlier observational studies had linked diabetes to many problems of ageing, from memory loss and dementia to depression, falls, disability, and bladder trouble. How strong and how broad that link really was stayed uncertain.

The authors gathered the existing studies and combined their results in a meta-analysis, a method that pools data across papers. They weighed diabetes against the risk of this whole set of ageing-related conditions at once. The review gives doctors and planners a clearer sense of the extra burdens diabetes adds in later life.
plos-pone-0004244:
Esteve Fernández and colleagues published this public health study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Spain's smoke-free law took effect on 1 January 2006 and covered all enclosed workplaces. Hospitality venues were the exception: owners could choose a full ban, partial restriction with smoking areas, or no restriction at all.

The team followed hospitality workers over time, measuring their exposure to second-hand smoke and their respiratory health. The cohort study tests what a partial law does for the workers it leaves unprotected. Its evidence bears on whether exemptions undo the benefits of smoke-free laws.
plos-pone-0004344:
John Kenny and colleagues published this microbiology study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Staphylococcus aureus is a common human commensal and opportunistic pathogen behind a wide range of infections. The team studied how S. aureus responds to these fatty acids and survives them. Understanding the bacterium's survival tricks matters for its virulence. Skin's natural antibiotics only work if the target cannot adapt, and this study checks that adaptation.
plos-pone-0004444: In 2009, Gálvez, San Martín, and Rodríguez found inflammation calling in reinforcements. TNF-alpha attracted mesenchymal precursors to white adipose tissue in obese mice. The signal summoned stem cells to fat. The finding links inflammation to obesity. The ob/ob mice modeled the process.
plos-pone-0004544: In 2009, Solé, Bonifaci, and López-Bigas found cancer gene lists largely agreeing. Biological convergence of cancer signatures was demonstrated. plos-pone-0004644: In 2009, Choi, Beattie, and Bryson argued big trials may miss a pain technique's value. Effects of neuraxial blockade may be difficult to study using large randomized trials. The rare complications need huge samples. The paper informs trial design. The blockade is spinal.
plos-pone-0004744: In 2009, a team found cat leukemia threatening the Iberian lynx anew here. Cat leukemia virus and other germs hit the rare wild cat. The captive breeding program fought back fast. The study informs wildlife rescue efforts. The lynx is Earth's rarest cat.
gi-bill-1944:

Critics note that Black veterans often faced blocks at the local level. A grateful nation's check still ranks among its best investments ever made. coke-institutes-part4-1644:

He surveys courts from Parliament and the great courts at Westminster down to local and special tribunals. For each, he gives its powers, its officers, and its limits. The survey doubles as a defense of the common law courts against rival royal courts of his own day. Read as a whole, the volume is the constitution of England in legal dress, an institutional map drawn by the man who knew the terrain best. It completes Coke's great design for the Institutes.
turgot-oeuvres-daire-vol1-1844:

It ended while the conference was still sitting, giving the letter a place in two stories at once.
frus-1945-50-intel-d44: A White House memorandum dated 7 November 1945 sits among the department papers of the intelligence volume. Papers from the president's house carry special weight in such a run. Since every department knew the final choice on a central intelligence system would be made there. The title gives no author, so the paper stands on its origin and date. Written while the Budget Bureau's plan was gaining ground in the autumn contest of 1945.
frus-1945-50-intel-d144:
Formal minutes cover the Second Meeting of the Intelligence Advisory Board, held on 26 March 1946. It survives in print as document 144 of the State Department's Foreign Relations volume on intelligence, 1945 to 1950. Washington was still building a peace-time spy service, run for the moment by the National Intelligence Authority and the Central Intelligence Group.

As minutes, the text sticks to the business of the meeting: items raised, views stated in brief, and the choices the group reached. The brevity is the point: what the group did not settle, the minutes do not claim it did. To read it in place is to watch the Cold War state being assembled at desk level.
frus-1945-50-intel-d244:
A memorandum from Director of Central Intelligence Hillenkoetter reached the State–Army–Navy–Air Force Coordinating Committee on 22 October 1947. The State Department prints it as document 244 in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. The National Security Act had just taken effect. The CIA had replaced the old group, and the Council had just begun to meet.

The value of the form is its speed: a page or two, a clear ask, and a name at the top to answer for it. Kept in sequence, such memos form the true diary of the office that sent them. Alone it is a page; in sequence it is evidence of how a state taught itself a new trade.
frus-1945-50-intel-d344:
A memorandum dated 12 April 1948 links two senior offices. The sender was the Executive Secretary of the Intelligence Survey Group (Blum). The reader was Allen W. Dulles, Mathias F. Correa, and William H. Jackson. It survives in print as document 344 of the State Department's Foreign Relations volume on intelligence, 1945 to 1950. Across Washington, the new security bodies were moving from setup work to the real business of the Cold War.

A memo of this kind was the basic tool of office work at the top. It put a matter before a senior man and asked for a choice, a signature, or a view. The reply, if any came, would build on the points laid out here. Kept with its neighbors in the volume, it shows the new system being built one dated paper at a time.
frus-1861-d44:
George Dallas wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 2 May 1861. The dispatch is document 44 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

May was the month of change in London, as Dallas wound down and Adams arrived. Dallas kept reporting until the end of his term. His letters from those weeks give readers the view of a departing envoy, watching a crisis grow past his watch. The handover between Dallas and Adams was smooth, a credit to both men's care. Smooth handovers abroad spared Washington one whole class of needless worry.
frus-1861-d144:
On 17 August 1861, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote a further letter to William Dayton. It is document 144 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

The second Paris letter of that day takes up its own point in the file. Seward's desk rhythm, seen across the volume, was to clear each topic in turn. The pair gives readers a full day of the French agenda in miniature. A full day of French business in miniature still reads as a tidy piece of craft. Tidy craft in a crisis is rarer than bold words, and worth far more.
frus-1861-d244:
Writing from Washington on 8 July 1861, William H. Seward addressed James Shepherd Pike, the American minister to the Netherlands. The printed record keeps it as Document 244 in the President's message volume for 1861. The letter comes from the first summer of the Civil War, a time when each foreign capital watched the war with care.

Outbound letters like this one told the envoy what line to take and what to report back. Read in order with its neighbors, it shows diplomacy as daily work rather than grand speeches. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d44:
Writing from Washington on 4 April 1862, William H. Seward addressed Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. The printed record keeps it as Document 44 in the 1862 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs volume. By then, in the spring of 1862, a year into the war, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

Outbound letters like this one told the envoy what line to take and what to report back. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d144:
15 September 1862 brought Charles Francis Adams a fresh letter from Secretary Seward in Washington. The printed record keeps it as Document 144 in the 1862 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs volume. By then, in the summer of 1862, the war's second year, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

Outbound letters like this one told the envoy what line to take and what to report back. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d244:
Document 244 opens the French file of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume: a report dated 6 December 1861 from William L. Dayton, the American minister in Paris, to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington.

France under Napoleon III watched the American war with close, self-interested eyes, and Dayton's post was second in weight only to London. His reports tracked French talk of backing the South or pressing a truce. This early letter came as the Trent crisis with Britain still filled the news, and Paris waited to see how it ended. Dayton, a former senator from New Jersey, held the Paris post from 1861 until his death in 1864.
frus-1862-d344:
Two Seward dispatches to Paris are dated 10 November 1862, and the first is Document 344 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Both went to William L. Dayton, the American minister to France.

By 10 November, word was spreading that Britain would not join France in acting on the war. Seward's letters that day wrote from a position slowly strengthening. The Paris brief now turned toward what France might do alone, in Mexico or toward the South. This dispatch opens the file's late-autumn phase, after the crisis peak. Southern agents were active in Paris too, seeking loans, ships, and friends at court.
frus-1862-d444:
Hermann Kreismann, the American consul in Berlin, received this instruction from Secretary of State William H. Seward on 6 September 1862. It is Document 444 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Consuls handled the practical edge of foreign policy: shipping, seamen, trade papers, and the protection of citizens abroad. Kreismann, a German-born Chicago editor, served the Union in the Prussian capital alongside Minister Judd. An instruction addressed to a consul rather than a minister points to business of that practical kind. Letters like this widen the picture of wartime diplomacy beyond courts and cabinets, down to the offices where Americans abroad actually got help.
frus-1862-d544:
On 4 September 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward addressed this note to Roest van Limburg. It is Document 544 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the official record for the year.

Seward wrote as Lee's army crossed into Maryland and the government braced for the autumn crisis. His note to the Dutch minister kept the Washington end of the Netherlands file in order at a moment when larger matters pressed. The correspondence's subjects remained the standing ones of neutral trade and maritime right. There is a kind of reassurance in the file's regularity. Through the worst weeks of 1862, the letters between Seward and Van Limburg went back and forth like clockwork. The relationship they served never cracked.
frus-1862-d644:
On 27 November 1861 Townsend Harris wrote his last letter in this run of the Japanese file, addressed to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It is Document 644 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Four days after his previous dispatch, Harris wrote again from Edo, in the closing weeks of his mission. He would leave Japan the following spring. His health was broken by the post he had created. His final letters report the treaty system standing and the legation's affairs in order for his successor. The volume's Japanese strand thus ends where it began, with the first minister's own hand. It is a quiet, fitting close to the farthest-flung correspondence in the record of 1862.
frus-1863p1-d44:
On 13 December 1862, Judah P. Benjamin wrote to Edwin De Leon. Benjamin ran the Confederate state office in Richmond; De Leon was a Southern agent working in Europe. The letter is document 44 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

De Leon served the South as a roving hand in Europe, where the work mixed talks, print, and quiet deals. Benjamin's letters to such men carried orders and cash-side news from home. This one came in mid-December, as the year of the South's best hopes closed. It is part of the group of Confederate papers printed in the Union's record, a rare chance to read the foe's mail.
frus-1863p1-d144:
Charles Francis Adams closed a three-letter day with this dispatch of 3 April 1863 to Secretary of State William H. Seward. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 144 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

The last sheet of the day wound up a set sent at the height of the ship question. Adams's April mail is among the most tense in the volume, as Britain weighed whether to let Southern warships sail. This letter ends the 3 April three. It is a working piece of the watch that, in the end, helped keep the British fleet out of the South's hands.
frus-1863p1-d244:
To guide his minister in London, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote these orders on 23 July 1863 to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. They stand as document 244 of the 1863 volume. The document comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States, the government's own published record of Civil War diplomacy. It was one of 3 letters between the same men dated that day.

Adams was told to deal chiefly with Lord John Russell, the foreign secretary. Seward's letters armed him with facts and wording for those meetings. It was written in the month of Gettysburg and Vicksburg, twin Union wins that changed how Europe judged the war. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it forms part of the fullest record of how the Union handled its most dangerous foreign relationship.
frus-1863p1-d344:
On 29 December 1862, Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, sent this note to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington. It appears as document 344 of the 1863 diplomatic papers. The letter is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, the official series that publishes American diplomatic papers.

British ships stopped by the Union blockade, and British subjects held as prisoners, supplied much of London's complaint list. Lyons delivered those protests in formal notes like this one. Set in its place in the volume, it helps readers trace how two governments talked their way past repeated crises.
frus-1863p1-d444:
A dispatch dated 4 April 1863 went from Lord Lyons, the British minister in Washington to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The State Department later published the letter in its 1863 foreign affairs volume, laid before Congress with the President's message. The letter is one piece of the steady stream of notes that passed between the two governments in the spring of 1863.

Letters like this one were the tools of a quiet contest. The Union meant to keep Britain out of the war, and it made that case note by note. Trade ran through the whole exchange. British mills wanted Southern cotton, while Union officials watched every cargo for war goods bound to the South. It is a small, dated piece of a very large record, and it earns its place by keeping that record complete.
frus-1863p1-d544:
From Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington to Secretary of State William H. Seward: a letter dated 30 May 1863. The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the spring of 1863. The two men at the ends of this channel, Seward in Washington and Lyons speaking for Britain, wrote to each other almost daily.

What the page shows is process, not drama. Claims, protests, and replies moved back and forth until small disputes stayed small. Trade ran through the whole exchange. British mills wanted Southern cotton, while Union officials watched every cargo for war goods bound to the South. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1863p1-d644:
The 23 October 1863 mail between Washington and London included a letter from Charles Francis Adams to William H. Seward. Adams was the American minister in London, and Seward was Secretary of State in Washington. Adams in London was the Union's front line in Britain, pressing its case with the British government week after week. The letter was later printed in the 1863 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message.

The standing business of this channel was friction at sea. Union warships stopped British merchant ships, and each seizure could spark a formal protest. The formal tone can hide the tension, but the pace gives it away. Notes this frequent mean both capitals were watching each other closely. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
plos-pbio-0020044:
Gregor Rainer, Han Lee, and Nikos K. Logothetis studied how learning changes vision in monkeys for PLOS Biology in 2004. They recorded from the extrastriate visual cortex, an area that processes what the eyes see beyond the first entry point. The monkeys learned a visual task while the team tracked nerve cell responses.

As skill grew, the way these cells fired changed with it. That shows learning does not just add facts in high brain areas. It also retunes mid-level vision itself. The work helps explain why practice makes sights easier to pick out and judge. It gives a concrete case of the adult brain reshaping its own wiring through experience.
plos-pbio-0020244:
Justin Gage Crump, Mary E. Swartz, and Charles B. Kimmel studied throat cartilage in zebrafish in PLOS Biology in 2004. The hyoid cartilage supports the tongue area in fish and, in changed form, in humans too. It forms near a pouch of gut tissue called the endoderm.

The team found that this pouch must use integrins, the anchor proteins that grip surrounding material, for the cartilage to form right. That is a case of one tissue guiding another's growth through its anchors. The work shows development is a team effort between tissues, not a solo program in each one. Faults in such guidance may underlie some human jaw and throat birth defects.
plos-pone-0000144:
Daniel A. Beard and Hong Qian published this theory paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. It works on a question in thermodynamics, the physics of energy and heat, applied to chemical reactions. Specifically, it examines how the driving force behind a reversible process relates to the one-way flows of molecules in each direction.

These relationships sit under much of biochemistry, since cells run on reversible reactions near equilibrium. The authors sort out exactly how force and flux connect. The result gives modelers of metabolism and other chemical networks a firmer theoretical base, and it corrects loose assumptions that can creep into textbook treatments.
plos-pone-0000244:
Thomas Clausen and Katharina Ribbeck published this theory paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. During cell division, the spindle, a scaffold of microtubules, separates the chromosomes. Some spindles form without centrosomes, the usual organizing hubs, and are called anastral. The authors model how such spindles organize themselves.

Their model combines three ingredients: microtubules that grow and collapse, autocatalytic production of more microtubules, and a spatial signaling gradient. Together these produce an organized spindle from disorder. The work shows how cells can build precise machinery by self-organization, without a blueprint or a foreman.
plos-pone-0000344:
Clarence C. Tam, Sarah J. O'Brien, Irene Petersen, and colleagues published this epidemiology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Guillain-Barré syndrome is a paralyzing autoimmune condition often triggered by infection. Using the UK General Practice Research Database, the authors examine how often it follows infection with Campylobacter, influenza, or Epstein-Barr virus.

Campylobacter food poisoning was the prime suspect, but numbers per infection were fuzzy. A huge practice database gives rates grounded in routine care records. The estimates help doctors counsel patients and help researchers weigh how much of the syndrome each infection explains.
plos-pone-0000444:
Gregory M. Mikkelson, Andrew Gonzalez, and Garry D. Peterson reported a link between wealth gaps and species loss, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Their study found that economic inequality predicts biodiversity loss, meaning places with wider gaps between rich and poor tend to lose more of their species.

The connection runs against the hope that growth alone saves nature. If inequality itself drives loss, through land pressure, weak protection, or short-term extraction, then social policy becomes conservation policy. Cross-country patterns like this one are early evidence, not proof of cause. Still, they reframe the problem. Protecting species may require narrowing inequality, not just funding parks.
plos-pone-0000544:
Santhi K. Ganesh and colleagues searched blood proteins for a signature of dangerous clots, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Venous thromboembolism, clots forming in veins, can travel to the lungs and kill, yet diagnosis often needs imaging that is slow or unavailable. The team worked on detection by proteomic serum biomarkers, patterns of proteins in blood serum.

A blood test for clots would speed triage of patients with chest pain or swollen legs. Proteomics screens thousands of proteins at once to find the pattern that separates patients with clots from those without. Studies like this are the discovery phase of test development, where candidate markers are found before validation.
plos-pone-0000644:
Lee Shaish, Avigdor Abelson and Baruch Rinkevich used a branching coral to ask how far flexibility can go, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Phenotypic plasticity is the ability of one genotype to adjust its shape and life traits to changing conditions. Their model animal is Stylophora pistillata, a coral that builds colonies by branching.

The researchers propagated colony pieces and watched how new branches formed, a process called astogeny. Some architectural rules stayed fixed while others bent with conditions. Sorting the fixed rules from the plastic ones shows what a colony can change and what it cannot. Reef biologists get a sharper sense of how corals cope with varied seas.
plos-pone-0000744:
Jon E. Brommer, Mark Kirkpatrick, Anna Qvarnström and colleagues measured whether fit parents of one sex predict fit offspring of the other. In PLOS ONE in 2007, they tackled the genetic benefits of mate choice in the wild. Those benefits are limited by how strongly male and female fitness are genetically correlated. A small or negative correlation breaks the logic of choosing a fit mate.

Their subject is lifetime fitness, total reproductive success across a life, measured outside the lab. If high-fitness males tend to produce low-fitness daughters, sexual selection faces a genetic tug-of-war. Knowing the correlation's true size changes what mate choice can and cannot achieve in evolution.
plos-pone-0000844:
Sushant K. Kachhap, Dennis Faith, David Z. Qian and colleagues assigned a new job to a gene whose loss tracks with spreading cancer, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Cell-to-cell adhesion is mediated by molecules on the cell surface, and downregulation of adhesion complex molecules is a characteristic of metastatic cancer cells. Downregulation of the gene NDRG1 increases metastasis in prostate and breast cancers, as background work showed.

Their title reports that NDRG1 is a Rab4a effector involved in vesicular recycling of E-cadherin, the main adhesion molecule between epithelial cells. Recycling returns E-cadherin to the surface after use. If NDRG1 helps that loop, losing it loosens cells for metastasis.
plos-pone-0000944:
Shojiro Kitajima, Yasusei Kudo, Ikuko Ogawa and colleagues showed how a chemical tag can stabilize a cancer linked protein, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Aurora-A is an enzyme that helps cells divide, and it is overproduced in many human cancers. Extra copies of its gene explain only part of that excess.

The team report that steady phosphorylation, a phosphate tag at one site, Ser51, keeps Aurora-A from being broken down. A stabilized protein piles up even without extra gene copies. That mechanism widens the list of ways a cancer cell can boost a growth driver. It also marks the tagging step as a point where a drug might intervene.
plos-pone-0001044:
Ravi Kolla, Suresh Chintalapati, Mojgan Sabet and colleagues boosted an anthrax vaccine by attaching an immune helper, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Anthrax is caused by Bacillus anthracis, and its toxins enter cells through a part called protective antigen. The standing vaccine relies on that antigen with an aluminum adjuvant and gives a slow response.

The team conjugated protective antigen to C3d, a fragment of the complement system that flags material for immune attention. Their title reports a rapid, sustained and protective antibody response. A faster anthrax vaccine matters for responders after an exposure, when weeks of waiting are not available.
plos-pone-0001144:
Cells constantly take in material from their surroundings through a process called endocytosis. Michela Felberbaum-Corti and co-authors examined one protein involved in the fluid-phase version of this uptake, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The protein is TXNL1, which the authors describe as a redox sensor, a molecule that reacts to the cell's oxidation state.

The paper also touches on Rab proteins, small switches that organize membrane traffic and are handled by a carrier called GDI. The authors report that TXNL1 plays a regulatory role in fluid-phase endocytosis. The work ties the cell's redox balance to its basic housekeeping of taking in fluid.
plos-pone-0001244:
High blood pressure runs in populations, and modern migration mixes ancestries in ways that can help locate the responsible genes. Xiaofeng Zhu and Richard Cooper used that strategy, called admixture mapping, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. They genotyped a panel of 2,270 ancestry-informative markers in a random sample.

The authors report evidence associating the VNN1 gene with hypertension. VNN1 codes for an enzyme called pantetheinase, not an obvious blood pressure suspect. Admixture mapping exploits the fact that a disease commoner in one ancestral group points to genome regions inherited from that group.
plos-pone-0001344:
Many obese people try diets; some lose weight and many do not, and nobody can tell in advance who will respond. David Mutch and colleagues asked whether gene expression in fat tissue, measured before weight loss, can make that prediction, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The ability to identify dietary responders in advance would change disease management.

The authors report that adipose gene expression prior to weight loss can differentiate and weakly predict dietary responders. Weak prediction is still a proof of principle: the fat's transcriptional state holds information about the future. Their study is an early step toward personalized diet advice based on biology.
plos-pone-0001444:
Jesús Lemus and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on drug residues that reach wild birds. Drugs given to farm animals can stay in dead stock left in fields. Scavenger birds that feed on those bodies may take in the drugs. The team checked blood of wild scavengers for residues of a common class of germ drugs.

They found marks of these drugs in the birds, tied to disease in some cases. The work warns that farm drug use can harm wild life far from the farm. Vultures and like birds have crashed in some regions for drug linked causes. The study adds proof for tighter rules on which drugs dead stock may carry.
plos-pone-0001544:
Takashi Hiroyama and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on making red blood cells in the lab. Donor blood supply falls short in many lands. A cell line that could make transfusable red cells in bulk would be a prize. No such line yet existed. The team tested whether mouse embryo stem cells could yield one.

They built lines of young red cell stock from the stem cells. Those lines could make working red blood cells on demand. That is a proof of concept for lab grown blood. Much work stays before human use, but the path is now shown to exist.
plos-pone-0001644:
Marcel M. Daadi, Anne-Lise Maag, and Gary K. Steinberg built a human neural stem cell line for stroke repair research, described in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. The cells came from human embryonic stem cells, which can supply nerve cells in near-limitless amounts. Grown in a flat, adherent culture, the line could renew itself and still mature into nerve cell types.

The team tested the cells in an experimental stroke model, grafting them into damaged brain tissue. The full text gives the culture method, the markers the cells carried, and how the grafts fared in the injured brains. A stable, well-defined cell line matters because stroke trials need cells that behave the same way in every batch. This work is an early step toward cell therapy for stroke damage.
plos-pone-0001744:
Philip E. Higuera, Linda B. Brubaker, Patricia M. Anderson, and their co-authors read ancient fire records in Arctic Alaska in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Feedbacks between land and atmosphere matter for predicting global change, above all in the fast-warming Arctic. Fire is a key process, but what altered fire regimes do to tundra was poorly known.

From paleorecords, traces preserved in lake sediments, the team found that fires were frequent in ancient shrub tundra. The full text gives the sediment cores, the fire dates, and how past fire frequency compares with today. A fiery past for the tundra suggests modern warming could bring back frequent burns, with large effects on carbon stores and northern ecosystems.
plos-pone-0001844:
Keng Boon Wee and co-authors studied how RNA folding affects a Duchenne muscular dystrophy therapy in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Antisense oligonucleotides, short synthetic DNA-like strands, can make cells skip faulty exons in the dystrophin gene, a potential therapy for Duchenne. Finding effective target sites was unsatisfactory because binding accessibility could not be predicted precisely.

The team shows that the dynamics of co-transcriptional pre-mRNA folding, how the RNA folds as it is being made, influence the induction of exon skipping. The full text gives the folding analysis and the skipping efficiencies. Better target prediction could turn exon skipping from trial and error into a designable drug approach.
plos-pone-0001944:
Daisuke Matsuzawa and co-authors measured a protective chemical in the brains of people with schizophrenia, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The chemical, glutathione, is a major guard against cell damage inside cells. It also plays a part in signaling through NMDA receptors, a path thought to go wrong in this illness.

Using a strong magnet scan that can read brain chemistry, the team measured glutathione in a rear midline area of the frontal lobe. As the title states, lower levels tracked with worse negative symptoms, such as flat affect and low drive. A chemical link to symptom load could guide new treatment ideas.
plos-pone-0002044:
Peter Ungar, Frederick Grine, and Mark Teaford read diet from the tooth wear of an ancient human kin, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Paranthropus boisei, a hominin from the Plio-Pleistocene, had huge flat cheek teeth with thick enamel. It also had a robust skull and jaw, and signs of massive chewing muscles. That build earned it the nickname Nutcracker Man.

The trio examined dental microwear, the tiny pits and scratches meals leave on teeth. Wear can test whether the teeth were used as nutcrackers in daily life, or only as a fallback for hard foods in lean times. Fossil diet is read from such marks.
plos-pone-0002144:
Deborah French, Wenjian Yang, Leo Hamilton, and co-authors compared gene activity in cancer cells and healthy blood cells, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. They asked how far gene activity matches between unlike tissues inside the same person. Their idea was that genes whose activity rises and falls together across tissues are more likely to be steered by inherited DNA differences.

The team looked at leukemia cells alongside normal white blood cells from the same people. Shared patterns pointed them to nearby DNA variants, called cis-SNPs, carried from birth. Findings like these help explain why the same gene can behave in unlike ways in different patients.
plos-pone-0002244:
Marjolijn Hoekert, Leonie Bais, René Kahn, and co-authors timed the brain's response to emotion in the voice, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Tone of voice, or prosody, tells listeners a speaker's feelings and intent beyond the words themselves. Earlier studies had pointed to the right frontal and right temporal parts of the brain as key sites for reading that tone.

The team mapped the time course of activity in the right anterior superior temporal gyrus and the right fronto-parietal operculum. Knowing which area acts first helps model how the brain builds an emotional read of speech, step by step, within fractions of a second.
plos-pone-0002344:
Paolo Sordino, Nikos Andreakis, Euan Brown, and co-authors used natural variation in a sea squirt to map mutant traits, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Ascidians such as Ciona intestinalis are simple chordates whose study has taught much about the origin of vertebrates. Forward genetics in Ciona, finding genes from their effects, needs richer information on how traits vary.

The team combined natural variation with model mutant phenotypes, traits from known laboratory mutants, to support that mapping. Wild populations carry ready-made differences that can pinpoint the genes behind a trait. The approach strengthens Ciona as a genetic model for the earliest branches of our own phylum.
plos-pone-0002444:
Research by Qi and co-authors came out in PLOS ONE in 2008. The author list runs from Zhen Qi, Gary W. Miller, Eberhard O. Voit, and others. Its subject is computational Systems Analysis of Dopamine Metabolism. A prominent feature of Parkinson's disease (PD) is the loss of dopamine in the striatum.

What the team did, and why they did it that way, forms the core of the piece. It stands as one careful step in a longer line of work, with its question and approach laid out in full. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002544:
Gratwicke and colleagues set out their study in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. The author list runs from Brian Gratwicke, Judy Mills, Adam Dutton, and others. Its subject is attitudes Toward Consumption and Conservation of Tigers in China. A heated debate has recently emerged between tiger farmers.

Each part of the study builds on the part before it, in the order the team carried it out. In short, the piece gives a clear, short route into a field that can seem hard to enter from the outside. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002644:
Work by Irene Sendiña-Nadal and colleagues appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008, dealing with phase locking induces Scale-Free topologies in networks of coupled oscillators. The catalog record names Irene Sendiña-Nadal first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. An initial unsynchronized ensemble of networking phase oscillators is further subjected to a growing process where a set of forcing oscillators. For readers, the value lies in how plainly the abstract sets out the problem and what the authors set out to test or describe.
plos-pone-0002744:
Research from Carsten Matz and co-authors, published in PLOS ONE in 2008, covers marine biofilm bacteria evade eukaryotic predation by targeted chemical defense. Authorship is credited in the record to Carsten Matz and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. Many plants and animals are defended from predation or herbivory by inhibitory secondary metabolites. Its abstract frames the work for later readers, who can judge the full text against the aims stated at the start. No results or figures are claimed in this summary beyond what the title and abstract themselves state.
plos-pone-0002844:
Work by Barbara Köhler and colleagues appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was bid participates in genotoxic Drug-Induced apoptosis of HeLa cells and is essential for death receptor ligands' apoptotic and synergistic effects. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Barbara Köhler, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. The BH3-only protein Bid is an important component of death receptor-mediated caspase activation. The authors add a further point. Bid is cleaved by caspase-8 or -10 into t-Bid, which translocates to mitochondria and triggers the release of caspase-activating factors.
